title: Observability
description: Telemetry primitives, service-level objectives, and actionable alerting architectures for understanding complex distributed state.

subtopics.title: Metrics
subtopics.subtitle: Numeric time-series aggregations, cardinality management, and histogram quantiles for low-overhead system health tracking.
keyTakeaways: Metrics are pre-aggregated numeric time series (Counters, Gauges, Histograms) optimized for fast querying, dashboards, and real-time alerting at constant storage cost per label set.
Unbounded label cardinality (e.g., attaching user_id or request_id as metric tags) causes time-series explosion, overwhelming TSDB index memory and compaction.
Always prefer Histograms over pre-computed client-side Summaries when aggregating latency across horizontally scaled instances so p95/p99 quantiles can be mathematically merged.

sections.heading: Metric Primitives & Aggregation Mathematics
sections.body: Time-series databases (TSDBs) store data streams identified by a metric name and a unique set of key-value labels. Unlike raw events, metrics compress millions of requests into compact numeric counters or bucketed histograms, decoupling storage footprint from traffic volume.
bullets: Counter: Monotonically increasing value (e.g., http_requests_total) reset only on process restart; queried via rate() or increase().
Gauge: Point-in-time snapshot that can go up or down (e.g., memory_in_use_bytes, active_connections, queue_depth).
Histogram: Samples observations into configurable upper-bound buckets (_bucket{le='0.1'}) plus _sum and _count, enabling server-side quantile estimation across fleets.

codeSnippet.title: Prometheus Histogram Instrumentation & PromQL p99 Calculation

sections.heading: The Cardinality Explosion Problem & TSDB Storage Internals
sections.body: Modern TSDBs like Prometheus use an inverted index in memory mapping label pairs to series IDs, backed by Gorilla XOR-compressed 2-hour blocks on disk. Total active time series equals the Cartesian product of all unique label values.
bullets: Cartesian Multiplicative Risk: 50 services x 30 endpoints x 10 status codes x 20 pods = 300,000 series (healthy). Adding a customer_tier (5) is fine, but adding user_id (10M) creates trillions of series and OOMs the TSDB.
Recording Rules: Pre-compute expensive high-fanout PromQL aggregations into lower-cardinality rolled-up series at fixed intervals.
Downsampling & Retention Tiers: Keep raw 15s resolution for 14 days, 5m rollups for 90 days, and 1h rollups for 1+ years in object storage.

tradeOffs.pros: Centralized scrape rate control, built-in target up/down health discovery, no collector overload loops during traffic spikes.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires service discovery visibility into target networks; ephemeral serverless jobs may exit before being scraped.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Kubernetes clusters, long-running microservices, and infrastructure daemon monitoring.

tradeOffs.pros: Works seamlessly with short-lived lambdas, batch jobs, and firewalled edge nodes without ingress ports.
tradeOffs.cons: Runaway clients can DDoS the central ingestion pipeline during retry storms without strict edge rate limiting.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Serverless functions, mobile/IoT telemetry, and multi-VPC environments without mesh routing.

subtopics.interviewTip: When designing a metrics pipeline in an interview, explicitly mention bounding label cardinality (never put user IDs or raw URLs in labels) and explain why server-side Histograms are required instead of averaging individual pod p99s.

subtopics.title: Logs
subtopics.subtitle: Structured high-cardinality event streams, inverted-index vs object-store architectures, and log ingestion pipelines.
keyTakeaways: Always emit structured JSON logs enriched with trace_id, span_id, service, and version so machines can query fields without fragile regex parsing.
Decouple application execution from log I/O by writing to stdout/stderr and letting node-level agents (Vector, Fluent Bit) buffer, batch, and ship asynchronously.
Separate hot full-text indexed logs (7-14 days in OpenSearch/ClickHouse) from cold object-storage archives (S3 + Parquet) to prevent observability bills from exceeding compute costs.

sections.heading: Structured Logging & Asynchronous Collection Pipelines
sections.body: Logs capture discrete, immutable records of high-cardinality events (including specific user IDs, stack traces, and payload metadata). Synchronous disk or network writes inside request threads can stall application event loops whenever downstream log collectors experience backpressure.
bullets: Zero-Allocation Structured Format: Emit newline-delimited JSON with standardized OpenTelemetry semantic conventions (timestamp, severity, trace_id, span_id, tenant_id).

Out-of-Process Collection: Applications write to container stdout; lightweight Rust/C DaemonSet agents (Vector, Fluent Bit) tail `/var/log/containers`, attach Kubernetes pod metadata, and batch-compress payloads.
PII Redaction & Sampling at Edge: Strip credit cards, JWTs, and emails in the collector pipeline before indexing, and dynamically sample verbose DEBUG/INFO health-check logs.

sections.heading: Storage Architectures: Inverted Indexes vs Columnar & Label-Indexed Stores
sections.body: Traditional full-text search engines tokenize every field into an inverted index, which provides sub-second needle-in-a-haystack queries but multiplies raw log byte size by 1.5x to 3x and requires expensive RAM-heavy clusters.
bullets: Full-Text Inverted Index (Elasticsearch / OpenSearch): Indexes every token in the JSON document. Ideal for arbitrary free-text search, expensive at multi-terabyte daily ingest.
Columnar OLAP Stores (ClickHouse): Stores log attributes in ZSTD-compressed columns with sparse primary indexes and bloom filters; achieves 10x compression and ultra-fast aggregations.
Metadata-Only Indexing (Grafana Loki): Indexes only low-cardinality labels (like Prometheus) and stores raw compressed log chunks in S3, relying on parallel brute-force grep over narrow time windows.

tradeOffs.pros: Sub-second needle-in-a-haystack queries on any arbitrary field, UUID, or free-text substring.
tradeOffs.cons: High storage amplification, JVM heap pressure, and expensive shard rebalancing at multi-TB/day scale.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Security audit trails, low-to-medium volume critical transactional logs, and complex ad-hoc forensics.

tradeOffs.pros: 80-90% lower storage cost via high-ratio columnar compression and S3 backing; minimal index overhead.
tradeOffs.cons: Unindexed substring searches across wide time ranges require high-throughput chunk scanning.
tradeOffs.bestFor: High-volume microservice access logs, VPC flow logs, and cloud-native observability at petabyte scale.

subtopics.interviewTip: Highlight the cost trap of logging: at 100k RPS, logging 1 KB per request generates 8.6 TB/day. Propose tiered storage (ClickHouse/OpenSearch for 7 days, S3 Parquet for compliance) and dynamic sampling of 200 OK logs.

subtopics.title: Distributed Tracing
subtopics.subtitle: W3C Trace Context propagation, causal span DAGs, and head-based vs tail-based sampling strategies.
keyTakeaways: Distributed tracing reconstructs the causal Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of a single request across microservices, queues, and databases using a shared Trace ID and parent-child Span IDs.
Context propagation (W3C traceparent header) must cross both synchronous RPC boundaries (HTTP/gRPC) and asynchronous message broker envelopes (Kafka headers).
Tail-based sampling buffers complete traces in memory to guarantee 100% capture of errors and high-latency outliers while sampling only 1% of healthy baseline traffic.
subtopics.architectureDiagram:
Client Request
  | traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6...-00f067aa0ba902b7-01
  v
[API Gateway Span A: 0ms ======================== 180ms]
   |--> [Auth Service Span B: 5ms == 20ms]
   +--> [Order Service Span C: 22ms ============= 175ms]
           |--> [Postgres Query Span D: 25ms == 45ms]
           +--> [Payment RPC Span E: 48ms ======= 170ms (ERROR 504)]

Span Stream ---> [Consistent Hash Load Balancer (by trace_id)]
                       |
                       v
               [OTel Tail-Sampling Collector Pool]
               (Keep 100% if error/latency>500ms, else 1%)
                       |
                       v
               [Tempo / Jaeger / ClickHouse Trace Store]

sections.heading: Anatomy of a Trace & W3C Context Propagation
sections.body: When a request traverses 20 microservices, metrics tell you *which* service is slow, and logs tell you *what* error occurred locally, but only a distributed trace reveals the critical path, serial vs parallel fan-out, and N+1 sequential database calls caused by an upstream caller.
bullets: Trace & Span Hierarchy: A Trace is a tree/DAG of Spans sharing a 128-bit `trace_id`. Each Span has a 64-bit `span_id`, a `parent_span_id`, start/end monotonic timestamps, attributes, and status.

W3C Trace Context Standard: Propagated via HTTP/gRPC metadata header `traceparent: 00-<trace-id>-<parent-span-id>-<trace-flags>`, plus optional `baggage` for cross-cutting routing keys (e.g., `synthetic-test=true`).
Async Boundary Preservation: Producers inject `traceparent` into Kafka/SQS message headers; consumers extract it and link their processing span via `Parent` or `FollowsFrom` references.

codeSnippet.title: OpenTelemetry Context Propagation & Tail-Sampling Config

sections.heading: Head-Based vs Tail-Based Sampling Architectures
sections.body: Storing 100% of spans at high scale is prohibitively expensive. Sampling reduces storage cost while preserving statistical and diagnostic visibility, but the point at which the sampling decision is made fundamentally changes architecture.
bullets: Head-Based Sampling: The ingress gateway rolls a dice (e.g., 1%) and sets the `sampled=01` flag in `traceparent`. Every downstream service obeys the flag. Cheap and stateless, but misses 99% of rare errors.

Tail-Based Sampling: Services emit 100% of spans to a collector tier. A first-tier router hashes `trace_id` so all spans of a trace land on the same collector node, which waits 5-10s before deciding whether to persist the trace.
Exemplars: Attach a sampled `trace_id` directly to a Prometheus Histogram bucket observation so engineers can click from a p99 latency spike on a dashboard straight to the exact offending trace.

tradeOffs.pros: Stateless, zero collector buffering memory, minimal network egress from application pods.
tradeOffs.cons: Blind to whether a request will fail or stall downstream; captures only a tiny fraction of rare 5xx errors.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Ultra-high-QPS edge services where collector memory buffering is cost-prohibitive.

tradeOffs.pros: Guarantees 100% capture of anomalous traces (5xx errors, p99 latency spikes) while keeping storage low.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires trace_id-affinitized stateful collector pools and full span network transmission from apps to collectors.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Mission-critical payment, checkout, and multi-hop microservice architectures requiring high debuggability.

subtopics.interviewTip: If asked how to implement tail-based sampling at scale, explain that a two-tier collector architecture with consistent hashing on `trace_id` is mandatory so all spans belonging to the same trace arrive at the same stateful collector instance.

subtopics.title: RED Metrics
subtopics.subtitle: Request-scoped microservice health telemetry: Rate, Errors, and Duration for standardized service dashboards.
keyTakeaways: The RED method (Rate, Errors, Duration) measures the external user experience of request-driven microservices, contrasting with the resource-oriented USE method (Utilization, Saturation, Errors).
Standardizing RED metrics across every RPC/HTTP boundary lets teams auto-generate identical service dashboards and topology health maps without custom per-team queries.
Always partition Duration histograms by error status so fast-failing 500s do not artificially lower perceived p50/p99 latency.

Incoming Requests |      Microservice Boundary          |
----------------> |                                     |

  | - Duration         |                           | - Errors (HW/OS)   |
  +--------------------+                           +--------------------+

sections.heading: The Three Pillars of RED & Standardized PromQL
sections.body: Popularized by Tom Wilkie (Weaveworks/Grafana), the RED method provides a uniform black-box contract for every stateless or stateful request-handling service. When every service emits the exact same metric schema via middleware or service-mesh sidecars (Envoy), on-call engineers can diagnose unfamiliar services immediately.
bullets: Rate: The number of requests per second the service is handling (`sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m]))`).
Errors: The number of failed requests per second (`status=~'5..'` or gRPC codes `Unavailable`, `DeadlineExceeded`), expressed as a ratio of total Rate.
Duration: The distribution of time each request takes, tracked via histograms and evaluated at p50 (median experience), p95, and p99 (tail latency).

codeSnippet.title: Standardized RED Recording Rules in Prometheus
codeSnippet.code:
groups:
  - name: service_red_metrics
    interval: 30s
    rules:
      # 1. Rate (Requests per second per service)
      - record: service:http_requests:rate5m
        expr: sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))

      # 2. Error Ratio (5xx responses / total responses)
      - record: service:http_errors:ratio5m
        expr: |
          sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]))
          /
          sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))

      # 3. Duration (p99 Latency in seconds for successful requests)
      - record: service:http_request_duration_seconds:p99_5m
        expr: |
          histogram_quantile(0.99,
            sum by (service, le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{status!~"5.."}[5m]))
          )

sections.heading: RED vs USE Method & Avoiding Latency Masking
sections.body: While RED measures customer-facing work, Brendan Gregg's USE method (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) measures underlying hardware and OS resources (CPU, disks, network NICs, thread pools). Together, they answer both 'Is the user impacted?' (RED) and 'Which resource bottleneck caused it?' (USE).
bullets: Fast-Fail Latency Distortion: When a database circuit breaker trips, requests fail in 1ms with HTTP 503. If 5xx responses are mixed into the latency histogram, overall p99 latency appears to improve during an outage!
Client vs Server RED Perspective: Emit RED metrics on both the server middleware and the outbound RPC client stub to immediately isolate network/load-balancer delays from application execution time.
Zero-Traffic Blind Spots: When Rate drops to 0 due to a DNS or ingress routing failure, Error ratio (`0 / 0 = NaN`) won't fire unless paired with a sudden traffic drop anomaly check.

tradeOffs.pros: 100% uniform RED metrics across polyglot services with zero application code changes.
tradeOffs.cons: Lacks application-level route templates unless configured; adds proxy CPU/memory overhead.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Platform engineering teams governing dozens of microservices in different languages.

tradeOffs.pros: Access to exact framework route patterns (e.g., `/users/:id`), internal business errors, and custom attributes.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires SDK version upgrades and enforcement across all application repositories.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Core services needing fine-grained endpoint attribution and semantic error classification.

subtopics.interviewTip: Point out the 'fast-fail paradox' in interviews: always compute Duration quantiles separately for successful (`2xx`) and failed (`5xx`) requests so a circuit-breaker outage returning instant 503s doesn't mask latency degradation.

subtopics.title: Golden Signals
subtopics.subtitle: Google SRE's Four Golden Signals: Latency, Traffic, Errors, and Saturation for holistic system observability.
keyTakeaways: The Four Golden Signals, Latency, Traffic, Errors, and Saturation, add capacity exhaustion visibility (Saturation) to request-level telemetry.
Saturation is a leading indicator of impending failure: systems degrade nonlinearly (via Little's Law and Kingman's queueing formula) once resource utilization crosses 80-85%.
Errors must encompass not just explicit HTTP 500s, but also implicit/semantic failures (e.g., HTTP 200 returning an empty fallback cart) and policy violations (responses exceeding SLA deadlines).
subtopics.architectureDiagram:
+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                  THE FOUR GOLDEN SIGNALS (SRE)                     |
+----------------+----------------+----------------+-----------------+
| 1. LATENCY     | 2. TRAFFIC     | 3. ERRORS      | 4. SATURATION   |
|                |                |                |                 |
| Success vs     | Demand load:   | Explicit (5xx) | Queue depth,    |
| Error p95/p99  | RPS, msg/sec,  | + Implicit     | DB conn pool %, |
| response time  | I/O bandwidth  | (bad payload)  | CPU run-queue   |
+--------+-------+--------+-------+--------+-------+--------+--------+
         |                |                |                |
         +----------------+--------+-------+----------------+
                                   |
                                   v
         [Queueing Inflection Point: Utilization > 85%]
         Saturation spikes ---> Latency explodes ---> Timeout Errors

sections.heading: Deconstructing the Four Golden Signals
sections.body: Defined in the Google SRE Book, the Four Golden Signals represent the minimum viable telemetry needed to understand the health and capacity of any user-facing distributed system. Specifically, adding **Saturation** bridges the gap between pure black-box request metrics (RED) and underlying capacity limits.
bullets: Latency: Time taken to service a request, strictly separating successful request latency from failed request latency.
Traffic: A measure of how much demand is being placed on your system (HTTP requests/sec, Kafka bytes/sec, active WebSocket sessions, or database transactions/sec).
Errors: Rate of requests that fail, either explicitly (HTTP 500, gRPC `INTERNAL`), implicitly (HTTP 200 with corrupt/empty fallback body), or by policy (response took longer than the hard 1s SLA).
Saturation: How 'full' your most constrained resource is, measured via queue depth, thread/connection pool occupancy, memory pressure, or CPU run-queue wait time.

codeSnippet.title: Monitoring Saturation & Queueing Inflection (HikariCP / Thread Pool)
codeSnippet.code:
# PromQL: Database Connection Pool Saturation Ratio
hikaricp_connections_active / hikaricp_connections_max > 0.85

# PromQL: Thread Pool Queue Wait Saturation (Leading Indicator of Latency Spike)
rate(executor_queued_tasks_total[1m]) > 0
and
(executor_active_threads / executor_pool_max_threads) > 0.90

sections.heading: Queueing Theory & Why Saturation Drives Tail Latency
sections.body: By Kingman's formula in queueing theory, expected wait time in a queue is proportional to $\frac{\rho}{1 - \rho}$, where $\rho$ is resource utilization. At 50% utilization, wait time is $1\times$ service time; at 90% utilization, wait time jumps to $9\times$; at 95%, it reaches $19\times$.
bullets: Leading vs Lagging Signals: Saturation (e.g., DB connection pool at 92% or Kafka consumer lag climbing) rises *before* p99 latency breaches timeouts and triggers cascading 504 errors.

Multi-Dimensional Saturation: A CPU-bound auth service saturates on CPU run-queue latency; an I/O-bound checkout service saturates on Postgres max connections or disk IOPS; an in-memory cache saturates on eviction rate.

Semantic Error Probes: Catch implicit errors by asserting business invariants in response middleware (e.g., incrementing `checkout_semantic_error_total` if an order confirmation lacks a transaction receipt ID).

tradeOffs.pros: Early warning before users experience timeouts; triggers auto-scaling proactively.
tradeOffs.cons: Can be noisy during brief, harmless micro-bursts that do not actually impact user SLOs.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Auto-scaling triggers, capacity planning tickets, and database connection pool protection.

tradeOffs.pros: Directly reflects real customer pain; zero false-positive pages when high utilization is benign.
tradeOffs.cons: Reactive, by the time p99 latency or 5xx rate spikes, the system may already be in a retry storm.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Paging on-call engineers via high-urgency PagerDuty alerts tied to SLO burn rates.

subtopics.interviewTip: In system design interviews, don't just list the 4 signals, identify the specific *Saturation* metric for each component you draw (e.g., 'For Redis, saturation is memory fragmentation/evictions; for Kafka, it is consumer partition lag; for Postgres, it is active connection pool ratio').

subtopics.title: SLI / SLO / SLA
subtopics.subtitle: Quantifying reliability through Service Level Indicators, Objectives, Contractual Agreements, and Error Budgets.
keyTakeaways: An SLI is a quantitative ratio of good events to valid events; an SLO is the internal target percentage for that SLI over a window; an SLA is an external legal contract with financial penalties.
The Error Budget (100% - SLO%) converts reliability from a subjective debate between Product and SRE into an objective, spendable currency for feature velocity and chaos testing.
In a serial dependency chain of N services, composite availability is the product of each component's availability, meaning downstream services must maintain stricter SLOs than the user-facing edge.

sections.heading: Precision SLI Formulation & Error Budget Governance
sections.body: Reliability is not binary; aiming for 100% availability is both mathematically impossible and economically wasteful. By defining explicit Service Level Objectives (SLOs), engineering teams align on how much unreliability is acceptable in exchange for rapid product innovation.
bullets: Event-Based vs Time-Based SLIs: Prefer event-based ratios (`good_requests / valid_requests`) over time-window uptime (`healthy_minutes / total_minutes`) so outages during peak traffic are weighted heavier than 3 AM blips.
The Table of Nines (30-Day Window): 99.0% (2 nines) = 7.2 hours downtime/month; 99.9% (3 nines) = 43.2 minutes; 99.99% (4 nines) = 4.32 minutes; 99.999% (5 nines) = 25.9 seconds.

Internal SLO vs External SLA Cushion: Always set the internal engineering SLO tighter (e.g., 99.95%) than the contractual customer SLA (e.g., 99.9%) to trigger corrective action before owing financial credits.

codeSnippet.title: Event-Based Availability & Latency SLI with Error Budget Math
codeSnippet.code:
# Good Events: Non-5xx responses that completed within 300ms
# Valid Events: All requests excluding client-side 4xx (except 429 rate-limits)

# PromQL 30-Day Rolling Availability SLI
1 - (
  sum(increase(http_requests_total{status=~"5..|429"}[30d]))
  /
  sum(increase(http_requests_total{status!~"40[0-4]"}[30d]))
)

# Remaining Error Budget Fraction (for a 99.9% / 0.001 error budget target):
# budget_remaining = 1 - ((1 - current_sli) / (1 - 0.999))

sections.heading: Composite Availability Math & Dependency Bounds
sections.body: A user-facing endpoint cannot be more reliable than its hard synchronous dependencies unless it implements fallbacks, caching, or circuit breaking. Understanding serial vs parallel reliability probability is essential for architectural sizing.
bullets: Serial Dependencies Multiply: If API Gateway (99.9%) synchronously calls Auth (99.9%), Order (99.9%), and Inventory (99.9%), the composite ceiling is $0.999^4 = 99.6\%$, violating a 99.9% edge SLO!

Redundant Parallel Dependencies Add: Two independent replicas or regions each with 99% availability fail simultaneously with probability $(1 - 0.99)^2 = 0.0001$, yielding $99.99\%$ composite availability.

Decoupling Hard Dependencies: To achieve a 99.99% edge SLO when calling a 99.9% third-party service, you must make the call asynchronous (queue) or serve stale cached fallback data during third-party outages.

tradeOffs.pros: Near-zero customer disruption; builds deep enterprise trust for critical financial or auth infrastructure.
tradeOffs.cons: Exponentially higher cloud cost (multi-region active-active), slower deployment velocity, strict change control.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Core identity/authentication, payment processing, DNS/edge routing, and control-plane primitives.

tradeOffs.pros: Generous error budget enables rapid CI/CD experimentation, single-region simplicity, and lower infra spend.
tradeOffs.cons: Allows up to 43 minutes to 3.6 hours of monthly degradation.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Internal tools, analytics dashboards, recommendation feeds, and batch reporting pipelines.

subtopics.interviewTip: Use composite SLO math during architecture reviews: if the interviewer asks for 'four nines (99.99%) availability,' calculate on the whiteboard how three serial microservices at 99.95% each drop overall availability to 99.85%, justifying why you need async queues or local caches.

subtopics.title: Alerting
subtopics.subtitle: Multi-window multi-burn-rate SLO alerting, alert fatigue prevention, and automated runbook triage.
keyTakeaways: Page humans only on actionable, user-facing symptom breaches (SLO burn rate); route cause-based or slow-burning saturation warnings to async tickets.
Multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerting pairs a long window (e.g., 1h) with a short confirmation window (e.g., 5m) to achieve fast detection and instant reset once an outage resolves.
Combat alert fatigue via deduplication, hierarchical inhibition (suppressing 50 microservice alerts when the core database or network switch is down), and mandatory runbook links.
subtopics.architectureDiagram:
Incoming Error Spike
          |
          +---> [Short Window: 5m Burn Rate > 14.4x] ---+
          |     (Confirms outage is STILL active now)   |---> [AND Gate] ---> PAGE ON-CALL
          +---> [Long Window:  1h Burn Rate > 14.4x] ---+     (2% budget      (PagerDuty)
                (Confirms statistical significance)            burned in 1h)

          +---> [Slow Burn: 6h & 30m Burn Rate > 6x] -------> [AND Gate] ---> PAGE / WARN
          +---> [Crawl Burn: 3d & 6h Burn Rate > 1x] -------> [AND Gate] ---> JIRA TICKET

sections.heading: Multi-Window, Multi-Burn-Rate Alerting Mechanics
sections.body: Static threshold alerts (e.g., `error_rate > 1% for 5m`) suffer from either poor precision (false positives on brief blips) or poor recall (missing a steady 0.5% error leak that exhausts a 99.9% monthly budget in 6 days). Google SRE's **Burn Rate** model measures how fast the service is consuming its 30-day error budget relative to a sustainable $1\times$ rate.
bullets: Burn Rate Definition: A burn rate of $1\times$ consumes 100% of the 30-day error budget in exactly 30 days. A burn rate of $14.4\times$ consumes 2% of the entire monthly budget in just 1 hour (exhausting 100% in 50 hours).

Why Two Windows (1h AND 5m) Are Required: Alerting solely on a 1-hour window means that after a 10-minute severe outage is fixed, the 1-hour average remains elevated for another 50 minutes, keeping the alert falsely firing.

Short Window Reset: Requiring *both* the 1-hour window AND the 5-minute window to exceed the $14.4\times$ burn threshold ensures the alert fires within minutes of onset and resolves within 5 minutes of recovery.

codeSnippet.title: Google SRE Multi-Window Multi-Burn-Rate Alert Rule (99.9% SLO)
codeSnippet.code:
# For a 99.9% SLO, allowed error fraction = 0.001
# 14.4x burn rate threshold = 14.4 * 0.001 = 0.0144 (1.44% error rate)
groups:
  - name: slo_burn_rate_alerts
    rules:
      - alert: HighErrorBudgetBurnPage
        expr: |
          (
            service:http_errors:ratio_rate1h > (14.4 * 0.001)
            and
            service:http_errors:ratio_rate5m > (14.4 * 0.001)
          )
          or
          (
            service:http_errors:ratio_rate6h > (6 * 0.001)
            and
            service:http_errors:ratio_rate30m > (6 * 0.001)
          )
        labels:
          severity: page
        annotations:
          summary: "High SLO error budget burn on {{ $labels.service }}"
          runbook: "https://runbooks.internal/slo/{{ $labels.service }}"

sections.heading: Alert Routing, Inhibition, and Fatigue Prevention
sections.body: When an underlying shared dependency (like a NAT gateway, core Postgres cluster, or Redis shard) fails, dozens of downstream services simultaneously breach their thresholds. Without intelligent alert topology routing, on-call engineers are flooded with hundreds of redundant pages.
bullets: Alert Inhibition & Grouping: Configure Alertmanager to group alerts by `cluster` and `namespace`, and inhibit downstream application alerts when a root-cause infrastructure alert (`DatabaseClusterDown`) is active.

Every Page Must Be Actionable: If an on-call engineer receives a page, looks at the graph, and goes back to sleep ('Oh, that always spikes during nightly ETL'), the alert must be deleted or converted into a non-paging ticket.

Automated Context Enrichment: Attach recent deployment diffs, top failing endpoints, and exemplar trace links directly into the PagerDuty/Slack payload to shave minutes off Mean Time to Detect/Mitigate (MTTD/MTTR).

tradeOffs.pros: High precision and recall; mathematically tied to customer SLOs; resets quickly after remediation.
tradeOffs.cons: Harder for junior engineers to intuit PromQL ratios compared to simple static thresholds; requires pre-computed recording rules.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Production Tier-0 and Tier-1 services with defined availability and latency SLOs.

tradeOffs.pros: Simple to configure and understand; works even on zero-traffic background workers.
tradeOffs.cons: High false-positive rate (CPU at 90% during GC or batch compression may have zero user impact), causing alert fatigue.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Stateful storage disk space (`disk_free < 15%`), certificate expiration, and dead-letter queue growth.

subtopics.interviewTip: Explain the difference between a 'Page' (wake a human at 3 AM because customers are actively burning >2% of the monthly error budget in an hour) and a 'Ticket' (handle during business hours because a slow burn will exhaust budget in 10 days).
